title: A sample of helium gas is placed in a free-moving gas syringe.
context:
The temperature of the helium is increased. The pressure of the helium does not change.

Which statement is correct?
options: The volume of helium decreases, and the helium atoms get closer together.
The volume of helium decreases, and the helium atoms get further apart.
The volume of helium increases, and the helium atoms get closer together.
The volume of helium increases, and the helium atoms get further apart.
answer: D. The volume of helium increases, and the helium atoms get further apart.
explanation:
Charles’s law: at constant pressure, the volume of a gas increases as its temperature increases.

Step-by-step reasoning

  1. Heating gives helium atoms greater average kinetic energy.
  2. More energetic collisions push the freely moving piston outwards.
  3. The volume increases while the number of atoms stays the same, so their average separation increases.

Check every answer

  • A. Both volume and spacing go the wrong way.
  • B. If the gas occupies less space, its average spacing cannot increase in this situation.
  • C. Expansion does not make the average spacing smaller.
  • D. Correct: expansion creates more space per gas atom.

Exam key idea: At constant pressure: higher temperature → greater gas volume → atoms farther apart.

title: Ammonia and hydrogen chloride diffuse from opposite ends of a tube. What is the first colour of the damp universal indicator, and which molecules move faster?
legend: Compare diffusion rates and indicator colours
context: Hydrogen chloride forms an acid in water; ammonia forms an alkali. Compare the molecules reaching the paper first.
explanation:
Diffusion: gas particles spread from regions of higher to lower concentration by random movement. At the same temperature, lighter gas molecules diffuse faster.

Step-by-step reasoning

  1. Calculate Mᵣ(NH₃) = 14 + 3(1) = 17.
  2. Calculate Mᵣ(HCl) = 1 + 35.5 = 36.5.
  3. Lighter ammonia molecules spread faster and reach the paper first.
  4. Dissolved ammonia forms an alkaline solution, so damp universal indicator changes towards blue.

Check every answer

  • A. Correct: the lighter alkaline gas reaches the indicator first.
  • B. Ammonia is alkaline; a red indicator shows acidic conditions.
  • C. Hydrogen chloride is heavier and slower than ammonia.
  • D. HCl would produce an acidic colour but is not the first to arrive.

Exam key idea: Lighter gas → faster diffusion. Ammonia is alkaline (blue); hydrogen chloride is acidic (red).
tableRows: Ammonia molecules move more quickly than hydrogen chloride molecules.
Ammonia molecules move more quickly than hydrogen chloride molecules.
Hydrogen chloride molecules move more quickly than ammonia molecules.
Hydrogen chloride molecules move more quickly than ammonia molecules.

title: A Group II metal forms an X²⁺ ion. Which quantity must have the greatest numerical value?
context: X²⁺ means the neutral Group II atom has lost two electrons.
explanation:
Nucleon number = protons + neutrons. A positive ion has fewer electrons than protons because it has lost electrons.

Step-by-step reasoning

  1. For Group II element X, the ion has p protons and p − 2 electrons.
  2. The nucleon number is p + n, the sum of protons and neutrons.
  3. The mass number exceeds either the proton count or the neutron count for a Group II atom, and it also exceeds the electron count.

Check every answer

  • A. Correct: it combines the numbers of protons and neutrons.
  • B. X²⁺ has lost two electrons, reducing its electron count.
  • C. Neutrons are only one part of the nucleon number.
  • D. The proton number is less than the total nucleon number.

Exam key idea: Mass number = protons + neutrons; a 2+ ion has lost two electrons.

title: Elements P and Q occupy the positions in the Periodic Table shown below. What formula will their ionic compound have?
explanation:
Group I atoms normally form Q⁺ ions and Group VII atoms normally form P⁻ ions.

Step-by-step reasoning

  1. Q loses one electron to form Q⁺.
  2. P gains one electron to form P⁻.
  3. One positive charge balances one negative charge, giving a 1:1 ratio.
  4. Write the positive ion first: QP.

Check every answer

  • A. Correct; 1 positive and 1 negative charge cancel.
  • B. Two Q⁺ ions would give a total charge of +1 alongside one P⁻.
  • C. Seven Q⁺ ions cannot balance one P⁻.
  • D. Seven P⁻ ions cannot balance a single Q⁺.

Exam key idea: Group I (+1) + Group VII (−1) → formula QP, not Q₂P or QP₇.

title: Which row is typical of a simple molecular substance?
legend: Recognise low melting/boiling points and low conductivity
context: The listed numerical values are illustrative property sets corresponding to the February/March paper concept.
options: Melts at −39 °C, boils at 357 °C, conducts electricity well
Melts at 3550 °C, boils at 4830 °C, poor conductor
Melts at 11 °C, boils at 181 °C, poor conductor
Melts at 97 °C, boils at 882 °C, conducts electricity well
answer: C. Melts at 11 °C, boils at 181 °C, poor conductor
explanation:
Simple molecular substances have weak intermolecular forces, giving comparatively low melting and boiling points, and normally lack mobile charge carriers.

Step-by-step reasoning

  1. Identify the expected combination: low melting point + low boiling point + poor conductivity.
  2. A and D are conductors, so they do not fit a typical simple molecular compound.
  3. B has extremely high melting and boiling points, suggesting a giant structure.
  4. C has low phase-change temperatures and is a poor conductor.

Check every answer

  • A. Conductivity is inconsistent with ordinary simple molecular compounds.
  • B. The very high temperatures suggest a giant structure.
  • C. Correct: relatively low temperatures and poor conduction.
  • D. It conducts well and has a high boiling point.

Exam key idea: Simple molecular = low melting/boiling points + generally no electrical conduction.

title: Diamond and silicon(IV) oxide have an important structural similarity. Which statement describes it?
legend: Identify the bonding arrangement in giant networks
context: Diamond is a form of carbon. Silicon(IV) oxide is written as SiO₂.
options: Both consist of separate molecules linked by weak attractions
Both consist of planes that slide across one another easily
Both consist of freely mobile positive and negative ions
Each carbon in diamond and each silicon in SiO₂ forms four covalent bonds
answer: D. Each carbon in diamond and each silicon in SiO₂ forms four covalent bonds
explanation:
Giant covalent structures are networks of atoms linked by strong covalent bonds throughout the solid.

Step-by-step reasoning

  1. Each carbon atom in diamond is covalently bonded to four other carbon atoms.
  2. In silicon dioxide, each silicon atom is covalently bonded to four oxygen atoms; each oxygen bridges two silicon atoms.
  3. This strong three-dimensional network explains their high melting points and hardness.

Check every answer

  • A. These substances are giant covalent structures, not separate small molecules.
  • B. Sliding layers describe graphite, not diamond or SiO₂.
  • C. They are not giant ionic lattices with mobile ions.
  • D. Correct: carbon and silicon each have four covalent bonds in their respective networks.

Exam key idea: Diamond: C bonded to 4 C; SiO₂: Si bonded to 4 O, O bonded to 2 Si.

title: Solid X is an ionic compound that does not conduct electricity. Solid Y is a metal that does conduct. Which statements about the solids are correct?
legend: Select the correct combination of statements
context:
1. X is a compound; Y is an element.
  2. Only X contains ions in a lattice.
  3. X contains positive and negative ions; Y has positive metal ions and no negative ions.
explanation:
Ionic solids: a lattice of fixed cations and anions. Metals: a lattice of positive metal ions with mobile delocalised electrons.

Step-by-step reasoning

  1. Statement 1 is true: the ionic compound X contains different types of ion; the pure metallic element Y has one type of metal atom.
  2. Statement 2 is false: metals also contain a regular lattice of positive metal ions.
  3. Statement 3 is true: the mobile delocalised electrons allow Y to conduct electricity.
  4. Choose 1 and 3 only.

Check every answer

  • A. Includes false statement 2.
  • B. Omits the true statement 3 and includes false 2.
  • C. Correct: only statements 1 and 3.
  • D. Includes false statement 2 and omits true statement 1.

Exam key idea: Both ionic solids and metals have lattices; metals conduct through delocalised electrons.

title: A student burns magnesium and calculates a theoretical yield of 10 g of magnesium oxide. Which expression correctly calculates percentage yield?
legend: Identify actual yield compared with theoretical yield
context: The theoretical mass expected is 10.0 g. The actual yield is determined experimentally.
explanation:
Percentage yield = (actual yield ÷ theoretical yield) × 100%. Both masses must use the same units.

Step-by-step reasoning

  1. Theoretical yield is the maximum expected product mass for the given reaction calculation: 10.0 g.
  2. Actual yield is the measured product mass.
  3. Divide actual by theoretical, then multiply by 100.
  4. Example: actual 8.0 g would give (8.0 ÷ 10.0) × 100 = 80%.

Check every answer

  • A. Relative masses are used in mole calculations, not directly as a yield ratio.
  • B. Compares product mass with starting magnesium mass, not the expected product mass.
  • C. Correct: measured product divided by theoretical product.
  • D. This describes a purity comparison rather than percentage yield.

Exam key idea: Percentage yield = actual ÷ theoretical × 100; percentage purity is a different formula.

title: 4.55 g of zinc is reacted with 50 cm³ of 2.25 mol/dm³ hydrochloric acid. Calculate the volume of hydrogen produced at r.t.p.
legend: Find the limiting reagent before calculating gas volume
context: Zn + 2HCl → ZnCl₂ + H₂
explanation:
A limiting reactant runs out first and determines the maximum product yield.

Step-by-step reasoning

  1. Zn: 4.55 ÷ 65 = 0.0700 mol.
  2. HCl: 50.0 ÷ 1000 × 2.25 = 0.1125 mol.
  3. 0.0700 mol Zn would need 0.140 mol HCl, but only 0.1125 mol is available. Therefore HCl is limiting.
  4. From 2HCl : 1H₂, n(H₂) = 0.1125 ÷ 2 = 0.05625 mol.
  5. Volume H₂ = 0.05625 × 24 = 1.35 dm³.

Check every answer

  • A. Correct: use HCl as the limiting reactant.
  • B. 1.68 dm³ is obtained by wrongly treating all zinc as the limiting reactant.
  • C. Too large: it misses the 2:1 HCl:H₂ ratio.
  • D. Too large: it assumes more hydrogen than either reactant can supply.

Exam key idea: Check the limiting reactant before using gas volume = moles × 24 dm³.

title: In the electrolytic apparatus shown, oxidation happens at electrode 1 and reduction at electrode 2. Which directions do electrons and positive ions move?
legend: Remember AN OX / RED CAT and cation migration
context: Electrode 1 = anode (+ in electrolysis); electrode 2 = cathode (− in electrolysis). The battery drives electron movement in the external circuit.
explanation:
Oxidation at the anode produces electrons; reduction at the cathode uses electrons. Cations move towards the negatively charged cathode.

Step-by-step reasoning

  1. At electrode 1, oxidation removes electrons from species and releases electrons into the external circuit.
  2. The power source transfers electrons through the circuit to electrode 2, where reduction consumes them.
  3. Positive ions in the electrolyte migrate towards electrode 2 (the negative cathode).
  4. Both directions are 1 → 2 as shown in the schematic.

Check every answer

  • A. Correct: electron transfer and cation migration are both towards electrode 2 in their respective paths.
  • B. Cations move to the cathode, not to the anode.
  • C. The overall electron-transfer direction is reversed.
  • D. Both directions are reversed.

Exam key idea: AN OX = oxidation at anode; RED CAT = reduction at cathode; cations → cathode.

Direction of positive ions in electrolyte

title: Which row states one advantage of a hydrogen–oxygen fuel cell and one advantage of a petrol engine?
legend: Evaluate the advantages of each energy source
context: The comparison concerns the gases released while the vehicle operates and the typical distance travelled before refuelling.
options: Fuel cell: longer range on one fill; petrol: no carbon dioxide in exhaust
Fuel cell: widely available hydrogen stations; petrol: no risk of fuel fires
Fuel cell: no CO₂ produced during its operation; petrol: typically greater range on a full tank
Fuel cell: no fire or explosion hazard; petrol: fewer refuelling stations
answer: C. Fuel cell: no CO₂ produced during its operation; petrol: typically greater range on a full tank
explanation:
A hydrogen–oxygen fuel cell combines hydrogen and oxygen to produce water and electrical energy. Burning petrol releases carbon dioxide.

Step-by-step reasoning

  1. The overall fuel-cell reaction is 2H₂ + O₂ → 2H₂O; there is no carbon dioxide in the reaction products.
  2. A petrol engine burns hydrocarbons, producing CO₂ during complete combustion.
  3. Petrol cars commonly have a longer range for a full tank than many hydrogen fuel-cell vehicles.
  4. Hydrogen is flammable and hydrogen filling stations are not as common as petrol stations.

Check every answer

  • A. Both claims are incorrect: range does not favour the fuel cell here, and petrol emits CO₂.
  • B. Hydrogen infrastructure is less widespread, and petrol is flammable.
  • C. Correct: fuel-cell exhaust is water; the petrol vehicle can travel farther between fuel stops.
  • D. Hydrogen has fire hazards; petrol has more widespread stations.

Exam key idea: Distinguish tailpipe emissions from full life-cycle impacts: hydrogen production can still generate CO₂.
tableRows: longer driving range on a full tank
no CO₂ produced at the vehicle
typically longer range between fuel stops

title: Which description best defines activation energy in a chemical reaction?
legend: Choose the definition of activation energy
context: Imagine a reaction profile with an energy barrier between reactants and products.
options: The greatest amount of energy that can be released by a reaction
The greatest amount of energy that a reaction can absorb
The least energy colliding reacting particles require for a successful reaction
The least energy released when new chemical bonds are formed
answer: C. The least energy colliding reacting particles require for a successful reaction
explanation:
Activation energy (Eₐ) is the minimum energy that colliding particles must possess for a reaction to occur.

Step-by-step reasoning

  1. A collision must have energy at least equal to the activation energy.
  2. On an energy profile, Eₐ is the vertical difference from the reactant energy level to the peak of the curve.
  3. A catalyst increases the reaction rate by providing a different route with lower activation energy.

Check every answer

  • A. Activation energy is a threshold, not the maximum heat released.
  • B. It is not the maximum energy absorbed in an endothermic process.
  • C. Correct: colliding particles need at least this minimum energy to react.
  • D. Making bonds releases energy, but this is not what activation energy means.

Exam key idea: Eₐ is measured from reactants up to the top of the energy barrier, not between reactants and products.

title: For 2H₂O₂ → 2H₂O + O₂, what is the enthalpy change, calculated using these bond energies?
legend: Calculate ΔH from bonds broken and formed
context:
Bond energies for the decomposition of hydrogen peroxide
BondBond energy / kJ mol⁻¹
O–H460
O–O150
O=O496
explanation:
ΔH ≈ total bond energy of bonds broken − total bond energy of bonds formed.

Step-by-step reasoning

  1. Broken: reactants contain four O–H bonds and two O–O bonds: 4(460) + 2(150) = 2140 kJ.
  2. Formed: products contain four O–H bonds in two water molecules and one O=O bond: 4(460) + 496 = 2336 kJ.
  3. ΔH = 2140 − 2336 = −196 kJ. The negative sign confirms an exothermic reaction.

Check every answer

  • A. −346 results from a bond-count or subtraction error.
  • B. Correct: the same four O–H bonds cancel, leaving 2(150) − 496 = −196 kJ.
  • C. The magnitude is right but the sign is wrong; more energy is released than supplied.
  • D. Both magnitude and sign are wrong.

Exam key idea: Bonds broken TAKE IN energy. Bonds made RELEASE energy. Negative ΔH means exothermic.

title: Which row identifies the conventional sources of nitrogen and hydrogen used in the Haber process?
context: The Haber reaction is N₂ + 3H₂ ⇌ 2NH₃. Choose the sources normally used in conventional large-scale manufacture.
options: Nitrogen from nitrate compounds; hydrogen from water
Nitrogen from nitrate compounds; hydrogen from methane
Nitrogen from air; hydrogen mainly from water electrolysis
Nitrogen from air; hydrogen mainly from natural gas (methane)
answer: D. Nitrogen from air; hydrogen mainly from natural gas (methane)
explanation:
In conventional ammonia production, nitrogen is separated from air and hydrogen is commonly made from natural gas, mainly by steam reforming methane.

Step-by-step reasoning

  1. Air is about 78% nitrogen, making it an economical source of N₂.
  2. Natural gas contains methane (CH₄), which reacts with steam to generate hydrogen-rich gas.
  3. Hydrogen can also be produced by water electrolysis, but it is not the usual conventional source described here.
  4. The product NH₃ is formed using an iron catalyst under suitable temperature and pressure.

Check every answer

  • A. Nitrogen is taken from air, not normally from nitrates.
  • B. Hydrogen may come from methane but the nitrogen source is wrong.
  • C. Air is correct, but electrolysis is not the usual feedstock route in this conventional process.
  • D. Correct: air supplies nitrogen and methane supplies hydrogen.

Exam key idea: Do not confuse the Haber reactant gases (N₂, H₂) with the industrial sources used to obtain them.

title: A white sample of anhydrous copper(II) sulfate is placed in contact with water. Which statement accurately describes the reaction?
legend: Distinguish anhydrous salts and hydrated salts
context: Anhydrous means without water of crystallisation; hydrated crystals contain water as part of their structure.
options: Anhydrous cobalt(II) chloride becomes blue when water is added
Anhydrous cobalt(II) chloride loses its water of crystallisation on heating
Anhydrous copper(II) sulfate becomes hydrated copper(II) sulfate when water is added
Blue anhydrous copper(II) sulfate turns white when water is added
answer: C. Anhydrous copper(II) sulfate becomes hydrated copper(II) sulfate when water is added
explanation:
White CuSO₄ (anhydrous) + water → blue CuSO₄·5H₂O (hydrated).

Step-by-step reasoning

  1. Copper(II) sulfate is white when anhydrous, and commonly blue as the pentahydrate.
  2. Anhydrous cobalt(II) chloride is blue and turns pink when hydrated.
  3. A hydrated salt can lose its water of crystallisation on heating, becoming anhydrous.

Check every answer

  • A. This reverses the cobalt(II) chloride colour change.
  • B. It is a hydrated salt, not an anhydrous one, that can lose water on heating.
  • C. Correct: the anhydrous salt takes in water to form a hydrate.
  • D. Anhydrous copper(II) sulfate starts white and becomes blue, not the reverse.

Exam key idea: Hydration colours: CuSO₄ white → blue; CoCl₂ blue → pink.

title: Acidified manganate(VII) ions react with iron(II) ions. Which row identifies the ion reduced and the reducing agent?
legend: Follow oxidation numbers and electron transfer
context: MnO₄⁻ + 8H⁺ + 5Fe²⁺ → Mn²⁺ + 4H₂O + 5Fe³⁺
answer: C. Reduced: MnO₄⁻; reducing agent: Fe²⁺
explanation:
Reduction = gain of electrons. A reducing agent supplies electrons to another species and is itself oxidised.

Step-by-step reasoning

  1. Fe²⁺ → Fe³⁺ + e⁻: iron(II) loses an electron, so it is oxidised.
  2. Mn in MnO₄⁻ changes from +7 to +2: it gains five electrons, so the manganate(VII) ion is reduced.
  3. Fe²⁺ donates electrons, so it is the reducing agent.

Check every answer

  • A. Fe²⁺ is oxidised, not reduced.
  • B. Both assignments are incorrect: Fe²⁺ loses electrons and MnO₄⁻ gains them.
  • C. Correct: MnO₄⁻ is reduced and Fe²⁺ is the reducing agent.
  • D. MnO₄⁻ is the oxidising agent, not the reducing agent.

Exam key idea: OIL RIG: oxidation is loss, reduction is gain. The reducing agent is oxidised.

chapter: Acids, Bases and Salts · Strong acids
title: Which pair of statements correctly describes aqueous hydrochloric acid?
legend: Identify statements about aqueous hydrochloric acid
context:
1. It is completely dissociated in aqueous solution.
  2. It turns thymolphthalein blue.
  3. It acts as a strong acid in water.
  4. It produces hydroxide ions as characteristic ions.
explanation:
Strong acid means the acid completely ionises in aqueous solution, producing hydrogen ions (more precisely hydrated hydrogen ions).

Step-by-step reasoning

  1. Statement 1 is true: HCl(aq) ionises essentially completely to H⁺ and Cl⁻.
  2. Statement 2 is false: thymolphthalein remains colourless in acid.
  3. Statement 3 is true: HCl is classified as a strong acid.
  4. Statement 4 is false: acids produce H⁺(aq), whereas alkalis produce OH⁻(aq).

Check every answer

  • A. Correct: 1 and 3 are both true.
  • B. Statement 4 wrongly attributes hydroxide production to acid.
  • C. Statement 2 is false because thymolphthalein is colourless in acidic solution.
  • D. Both selected statements are false.

Exam key idea: A strong acid is fully ionised; strong does not mean concentrated.

title: Which statements about the two dissociation stages of sulfuric acid are correct?
context:
H₂SO₄ ⇌ H⁺ + HSO₄⁻
HSO₄⁻ ⇌ H⁺ + SO₄²⁻

  1. HSO₄⁻ can donate and accept protons.
  2. H₂SO₄ can donate protons.
  3. SO₄²⁻ is the only base present.
explanation:
HSO₄⁻ is amphiprotic: it can accept a proton to form H₂SO₄ or donate a proton to form SO₄²⁻.

Step-by-step reasoning

  1. HSO₄⁻ can donate H⁺ to give SO₄²⁻ and accept H⁺ to give H₂SO₄. Statement 1 is true.
  2. H₂SO₄ is a proton donor, so statement 2 is true.
  3. SO₄²⁻ can accept a proton, but HSO₄⁻ can also accept one: statement 3 is false.

Check every answer

  • A. Correct: statements 1 and 2 describe proton transfer correctly.
  • B. Statement 2 is also true, so statement 1 alone is incomplete.
  • C. Statement 3 is false because HSO₄⁻ can also act as a base.
  • D. Statement 3 is false.

Exam key idea: HSO₄⁻ is both an acid and a base depending on whether it donates or accepts H⁺.

chapter: Acids, Bases and Salts · Amphoteric oxides
title: A solid oxide such as zinc oxide is described as amphoteric. Which pair of reactions is possible?
legend: Use the definition of an amphoteric oxide
context: Examples of amphoteric oxides in IGCSE Chemistry include aluminium oxide and zinc oxide.
options: It reacts with acids only, making salt and water
It reacts with both acids and bases, giving salts and water
It reacts with both acids and bases, making hydrogen gas in both reactions
It reacts with bases only, making salt and water
answer: B. It reacts with both acids and bases, giving salts and water
explanation:
An amphoteric oxide reacts with both acids and alkalis/bases to form salts and water.

Step-by-step reasoning

  1. With an acid: ZnO + 2HCl → ZnCl₂ + H₂O.
  2. With an alkali, ZnO also reacts; zinc-containing salts or complexes are produced, together with water in suitable equations.
  3. Releasing hydrogen from acid is characteristic of many metals, not a general feature of amphoteric metal oxides.

Check every answer

  • A. This describes a basic oxide, not an amphoteric one.
  • B. Correct: amphoteric oxides react with both types of reagent.
  • C. Metal oxides do not produce hydrogen as the usual acid–base product.
  • D. This describes an acidic oxide, not an amphoteric one.

Exam key idea: Amphoteric = reacts with BOTH acids and bases; examples: Al₂O₃, ZnO.

chapter: The Periodic Table · Across a period
title: Going from left to right through the main-group elements of Period 3, which property generally increases?
context: Period 3 runs from sodium to argon; every element has three occupied electron shells.
options: How many electron shells are occupied
The number of electrons in the outermost occupied shell
How easily atoms form positive ions
answer: C. The number of electrons in the outermost occupied shell
explanation:
Across a period, proton number and outer-shell electron count generally increase for the main-group elements.

Step-by-step reasoning

  1. Sodium starts with electron configuration 2,8,1 (one valence electron).
  2. Magnesium is 2,8,2; chlorine is 2,8,7; argon is 2,8,8.
  3. The shell count stays three across Period 3.
  4. Metallic character tends to decrease and non-metallic character tends to increase.

Check every answer

  • A. Metallic character falls rather than rises.
  • B. The number of occupied shells stays constant within one period.
  • C. Correct: valence electron count increases across the main-group sequence.
  • D. The tendency to lose electrons and make positive ions generally decreases.

Exam key idea: Period = number of occupied shells. For main-group elements, group position indicates outer electrons.

title: Which pair of compounds could be mixed as aqueous solutions to produce insoluble lead(II) chloride?
legend: Choose soluble reactants to make a precipitate
context:
The table gives water solubilities of four possible reactants. Choose the pair that can be mixed as solutions to produce a precipitate.

Possible reactants and their solubility in water
No.CompoundSoluble in water?
1lead(II) nitrateyes
2lead(II) sulfateno
3silver chlorideno
4sodium chlorideyes
explanation:
A precipitation reaction uses two soluble aqueous reactants to form an insoluble solid.

Step-by-step reasoning

  1. Lead(II) nitrate dissolves in water, providing Pb²⁺ ions.
  2. Sodium chloride dissolves in water, providing Cl⁻ ions.
  3. The ions combine: Pb²⁺(aq) + 2Cl⁻(aq) → PbCl₂(s).
  4. The suitable soluble reactants are 1 and 4.

Check every answer

  • A. Silver chloride (3) is insoluble, so it is not an appropriate dissolved reactant.
  • B. Correct: both 1 and 4 are soluble and supply Pb²⁺ and Cl⁻.
  • C. Both substances are insoluble, so they cannot be mixed as aqueous solutions.
  • D. Lead(II) sulfate is insoluble and unsuitable as an aqueous reagent.

Exam key idea: For precipitation, start with soluble salts and obtain an insoluble product.

title: Which combination of statements describes transition elements?
context:
1. They form only white compounds.
  2. They can be drawn into wires.
  3. They generally have high densities.
  4. They form positive ions by gaining electrons.
explanation:
Transition elements are generally ductile and have high densities; many of their compounds are coloured.

Step-by-step reasoning

  1. Statement 1 is false: transition-metal ions commonly form coloured compounds.
  2. Statement 2 is true: ductile means able to be drawn into wires.
  3. Statement 3 is true: transition elements are generally high-density metals.
  4. Statement 4 is false: metal atoms form positive ions by losing electrons.

Check every answer

  • A. Statement 1 is false; statement 2 is true.
  • B. Both statements are false.
  • C. Correct: statements 2 and 3 are true.
  • D. Statement 3 is true but statement 4 is false.

Exam key idea: Metals make cations by electron loss, not electron gain.

title: Why does aluminium resist further corrosion even though it reacts readily with oxygen?
context: Think about what happens to the metal surface when aluminium first comes into contact with air.
options: Its high chemical reactivity automatically prevents corrosion
A thin protective oxide film forms on its surface
It can react only when heated to a high temperature
It is chemically inert under all conditions
answer: B. A thin protective oxide film forms on its surface
explanation:
Aluminium rapidly forms a thin, tightly attached layer of aluminium oxide (Al₂O₃) that prevents further attack.

Step-by-step reasoning

  1. Aluminium does react with oxygen in air.
  2. Its oxide layer is adherent and helps block water and oxygen from the metal.
  3. Because the layer is protective, the underlying metal shows excellent corrosion resistance.

Check every answer

  • A. Reactivity alone does not prevent corrosion; it contributes to oxide formation.
  • B. Correct: the protective Al₂O₃ film is a barrier.
  • C. Aluminium can react at ordinary temperatures; it is not protected solely by high heat requirements.
  • D. Aluminium is not inert; it reacts readily but develops passivation.

Exam key idea: Passivation = a thin protective oxide layer forms on a metal surface.

title: Which protective coating will continue to protect iron if it becomes scratched or damaged?
context: A damaged coating may expose the iron to water and oxygen. Which coating is a more reactive metal than iron?
explanation:
Zinc is more reactive than iron, so it can provide sacrificial protection even when the coating is scratched.

Step-by-step reasoning

  1. Paint and plastic act only as physical barriers and cannot protect exposed iron after damage.
  2. Copper is less reactive than iron; in an electrolyte, contact with copper may accelerate corrosion of the iron.
  3. Zinc preferentially oxidises and protects nearby iron.

Check every answer

  • A. Copper is less reactive than iron and does not give sacrificial protection.
  • B. Paint protects only while its coating remains intact.
  • C. Plastic is a physical barrier and fails to protect exposed regions.
  • D. Correct: zinc is the sacrificial metal used in galvanising.

Exam key idea: Galvanising iron with zinc provides both barrier and sacrificial protection.

title: Which pair of statements about contaminants in water from natural sources is correct?
context:
1. Detergents contain nitrates that always cause disease.
  2. Untreated sewage can contain disease-causing microorganisms.
  3. All metal compounds are toxic.
  4. Fertilisers can add nitrates and phosphates that damage aquatic ecosystems.
explanation:
Sewage may contain pathogens and fertiliser runoff may cause eutrophication.

Step-by-step reasoning

  1. Statement 1 is false: it confuses typical detergent pollutants with nitrates and wrongly claims disease in all cases.
  2. Statement 2 is true: sewage can contain bacteria and other pathogens.
  3. Statement 3 is false: not every metal-containing compound is toxic.
  4. Statement 4 is true: extra nitrates and phosphates can cause algal blooms and oxygen depletion.

Check every answer

  • A. Statements 1 and 3 are not both true.
  • B. Statement 1 is false, although 4 is true.
  • C. Statement 3 is false, although 2 is true.
  • D. Correct: sewage pathogens and fertiliser nutrient pollution are both important.

Exam key idea: Nitrates and phosphates cause eutrophication; untreated sewage can spread disease.

title: The flow diagram represents the greenhouse effect. Which row correctly identifies stages X, Y and Z?
context: Follow the three labels in the question diagram and choose the matching row.
options: A. absorption → emission to Earth → less heat escapes
B. emission → emission to space → less heat escapes
C. absorption → emission to Earth → more heat escapes
D. emission → emission to space → more heat escapes
answer: A. A. absorption → emission to Earth → less heat escapes
explanation:
Greenhouse gases absorb infrared radiation emitted by Earth and re-emit thermal energy in all directions, including back toward Earth.

Step-by-step reasoning

  1. Earth emits long-wave infrared radiation.
  2. Greenhouse gases absorb some of this outgoing radiation (X).
  3. These gases re-emit some infrared towards Earth (Y).
  4. This reduces the net heat lost to space (Z), contributing to warming.

Check every answer

  • A. Correct: absorption, re-emission toward Earth, and reduced net loss to space.
  • B. The gases absorb Earth’s radiation before re-emitting it; the row misidentifies the first stage.
  • C. The first two descriptions are right, but increased energy loss would tend to cool Earth.
  • D. This reverses the absorption step and wrongly increases loss to space.

Exam key idea: Absorption + re-emission toward Earth → reduced net energy escape.

title: Which combustion equation produces two pollutants that are not normal constituents of clean air?
context: Look for two separate harmful products: carbon monoxide (CO) and solid carbon particles (soot).
explanation:
Incomplete combustion can form carbon monoxide (CO) and particulate carbon (C), both important air pollutants.

Step-by-step reasoning

  1. Option A gives CO₂ and water, not the two target pollutants.
  2. Option B gives CO but no carbon particulates.
  3. Option C gives carbon particulates but no carbon monoxide.
  4. Option D gives both 14CO and 4C, meaning carbon monoxide and soot are produced.

Check every answer

  • A. CO₂ is present at low levels in clean air and water is not the target pollutant here.
  • B. Only CO is one of the two pollutants requested.
  • C. Only soot is one of the two pollutants requested.
  • D. Correct: CO and C are produced together.

Exam key idea: Incomplete hydrocarbon combustion can generate carbon monoxide and soot.

title: Which pair of petroleum fractions can both be used as fuels for vehicles?
context: Consider road vehicles and aircraft as types of vehicles.
explanation:
Gasoline (petrol) is used for many road vehicles; kerosene is used as aviation fuel.

Step-by-step reasoning

  1. Fractional distillation separates crude oil into fractions with different boiling-point ranges.
  2. Gasoline is used to run many petrol engines.
  3. Kerosene is used in jet aircraft.
  4. Bitumen is mainly used for road surfacing; lubricating fractions for lubricants; naphtha is often chemical feedstock.

Check every answer

  • A. Bitumen is not normally a vehicle fuel.
  • B. Neither bitumen nor naphtha is the intended vehicle-fuel pair.
  • C. Correct: gasoline for vehicles and kerosene for aircraft.
  • D. Lubricating fractions are not principally vehicle fuels.

Exam key idea: Fuel uses: gasoline → cars; kerosene → aircraft; diesel → engines.

title: Butanoic acid reacts with ethanol. Which row correctly identifies the ester structural formula and its empirical formula?
legend: Identify ester linkages and simplify atom ratios
context: Use the displayed formula above to identify the acid chain before combining it with ethanol.
explanation:
Ethanol + butanoic acid forms ethyl butanoate with structural formula C₃H₇COOC₂H₅ and empirical formula C₃H₆O.

Step-by-step reasoning

  1. The reaction is butanoic acid + ethanol ⇌ ethyl butanoate + water.
  2. Ethyl butanoate has formula C₃H₇COOC₂H₅, which totals C₆H₁₂O₂.
  3. Divide all molecular subscripts by 2: C₆H₁₂O₂ → C₃H₆O.
  4. Choose the row containing the correct structural and empirical formulae.

Check every answer

  • A. The structural formula is right, but C₆H₁₂O₂ is the molecular formula, not the simplest ratio.
  • B. Correct: both the ester structure and empirical ratio match.
  • C. CH₃COOC₄H₉ is a different ester (butyl ethanoate) and the empirical formula is also not simplified.
  • D. The empirical formula is correct but the structural formula describes a different ester.

Exam key idea: The acid supplies the -COO- part of the ester; simplify molecular formula to get the empirical formula.

title: Which formula explicitly shows the structural arrangement of propan-1-ol?
legend: Distinguish molecular, structural and general formulae
context: A structural formula must show how the groups are joined, including the location of the alcohol functional group.
explanation:
Propan-1-ol has three carbon atoms in a straight chain, with the –OH group on the first carbon: CH₃CH₂CH₂OH.

Step-by-step reasoning

  1. Propan- means a 3-carbon chain.
  2. The ending -ol indicates an alcohol containing the –OH functional group.
  3. The number 1 says –OH is on an end carbon, so CH₃–CH₂–CH₂–OH.
  4. C₃H₈O is the molecular formula, while CₙH₂ₙ₊₁OH is the general formula.

Check every answer

  • A. C₃H₇OH gives its composition but does not clearly specify the carbon bonding arrangement or hydroxyl position.
  • B. Correct: this condensed structural formula identifies the chain and –OH position.
  • C. C₃H₈O is a molecular formula, not a structural formula.
  • D. CₙH₂ₙ₊₁OH is the general formula for monohydric alcohols.

Exam key idea: Structural formula shows atom connectivity, not merely overall atom counts.

title: Alkenes can undergo addition reactions with aqueous bromine, hydrogen or steam.
context:
Which reactions of ethene need a catalyst?

  1. with aqueous bromine
  2. with steam
  3. with hydrogen
explanation:
Ethene requires a catalyst for its reactions with steam and hydrogen, but not for its reaction with bromine water.

Step-by-step reasoning

  1. Reaction 1: ethene decolourises aqueous bromine by addition without a catalyst.
  2. Reaction 2: hydration of ethene with steam uses a phosphoric acid catalyst, producing ethanol.
  3. Reaction 3: hydrogenation of ethene uses a nickel catalyst, producing ethane.
  4. Therefore statements 2 and 3 only need catalysts.

Why each option is right or wrong

  • A. Incorrect: bromine water reacts without a catalyst.
  • B. Incorrect: steam needs a catalyst, but bromine does not.
  • C. Incorrect: both steam and hydrogen need catalysts.
  • D. Correct: steam uses H₃PO₄; hydrogen uses Ni.

Exam key idea: Bromine water: no catalyst. Steam: H₃PO₄. Hydrogen: Ni.

title: Which conditions are used to manufacture ethanol by fermentation?
explanation:
Fermentation uses yeast and warm conditions, commonly around 30 °C. Yeast enzymes catalyse the breakdown of sugars.

Step-by-step reasoning

  1. Glucose solution is mixed with yeast.
  2. A temperature of approximately 30 °C allows yeast enzymes to work efficiently.
  3. Oxygen is excluded or limited; glucose is converted into ethanol and carbon dioxide.
  4. At 300 °C the enzymes would be denatured and the yeast would not survive.

Why each option is right or wrong

  • A. 300 °C would kill the yeast and denature its enzymes.
  • B. 30 °C is suitable, but acid is not the fermentation catalyst.
  • C. 300 °C and an acid catalyst describe neither normal fermentation nor workable yeast conditions.
  • D. Correct: 30 °C with yeast.

Exam key idea: Fermentation: glucose → ethanol + carbon dioxide, using yeast at about 30 °C without oxygen.

title: Which statement about an aqueous solution of ethanoic acid is correct?
options: It reacts with magnesium to form water as one of the products.
It reacts with sodium carbonate to form carbon dioxide.
It reacts with sodium hydroxide to form hydrogen.
It turns red litmus paper blue.
answer: B. It reacts with sodium carbonate to form carbon dioxide.
explanation:
Ethanoic acid reacts with a carbonate to produce salt, water, and carbon dioxide.

Step-by-step reasoning

  1. Ethanoic acid is a weak acid, but it still shows the usual reactions of acids.
  2. Acid + carbonate → salt + water + carbon dioxide.
  3. With sodium carbonate: 2CH₃COOH + Na₂CO₃ → 2CH₃COONa + H₂O + CO₂.
  4. Acids turn blue litmus red; they do not turn red litmus blue.

Why each option is right or wrong

  • A. Acid + magnesium produces hydrogen gas, not water.
  • B. Correct: a carbonate reacts with the acid to release CO₂.
  • C. Acid + sodium hydroxide produces a salt and water, not hydrogen.
  • D. Acidic solutions turn blue litmus red (red stays red).

Exam key idea: Acid + carbonate → salt + H₂O + CO₂.

title: Which statements explain why plastics should be recycled?
context:
1. Most do not decompose when they are added to landfill.
  2. They pollute rivers and the ocean where they harm wildlife.
  3. They can produce toxic gases when they are burned.
explanation:
All three statements are valid reasons for recycling plastics.

Step-by-step reasoning

  1. Many common plastics break down extremely slowly in landfill.
  2. Plastic waste can enter rivers and oceans, harming organisms through entanglement and ingestion.
  3. Some plastics emit hazardous gases when burned, especially under uncontrolled conditions.
  4. Recycling can reduce waste and the need to produce new plastic.

Why each option is right or wrong

  • A. Correct: all three concerns are valid.
  • B. Incomplete: statement 3 is also correct.
  • C. Incomplete: statement 2 is also correct.
  • D. Incomplete: statement 1 is also correct.

Exam key idea: Recycling reduces persistent waste, wildlife harm, and pollution from disposal.

title: Which statements about the plastic PET are correct?
context:
1. PET is a condensation polymer.
  2. PET is a polyamide.
  3. PET can be converted into monomers and re-polymerised.
explanation:
PET is a condensation polyester, not a polyamide, and it can be chemically recycled.

Step-by-step reasoning

  1. PET is formed by condensation polymerisation, linking appropriate monomers to make a polyester.
  2. Its links are ester (–COO–) bonds, not amide (–CONH–) bonds.
  3. Chemical recycling can break PET into suitable monomers or intermediates for re-polymerisation.
  4. Statements 1 and 3 are true.

Why each option is right or wrong

  • A. Includes incorrect statement 2.
  • B. Statement 3 is true, while 2 is false.
  • C. Correct: statements 1 and 3 only.
  • D. Incorrect because statement 2 is false and statement 1 is true.

Exam key idea: PET is a polyester (ester links), not a polyamide (amide links).

title: The diagram represents part of the structure of a protein.
context:
Three atoms have been labelled X, Y and Z.

Which elements are X, Y and Z?
explanation:
X is oxygen, Y is hydrogen and Z is nitrogen. Use the typical bonding of each element.

Step-by-step reasoning

  1. X is double-bonded to carbon (C=O), indicating oxygen.
  2. Y is bonded once to N in the group –NH–, indicating hydrogen.
  3. Z is bonded to carbon on both sides and a hydrogen, making three covalent bonds; it is nitrogen.
  4. Thus X = O; Y = H; Z = N.

Why each option is right or wrong

  • A. X is not carbon and Z is not oxygen.
  • B. X cannot be hydrogen when it makes a double bond to carbon; Y is not oxygen.
  • C. Correct: O, H, N.
  • D. Z is nitrogen (three bonds), not carbon (typically four bonds).

Exam key idea: C makes 4 bonds; N makes 3; O makes 2; H makes 1.

title: Locating agents are often used in paper chromatography.
context: Which mixture requires a locating agent?
options: a mixture of two colourless substances
a mixture of two insoluble substances
a mixture of two different-coloured substances with the same R<sub>f</sub> value
a mixture of two substances that are the same colour
answer: A. a mixture of two colourless substances
explanation:
Colourless substances cannot be seen on the paper; a locating agent reveals their spots.

Step-by-step reasoning

  1. Separate the mixture by chromatography using an appropriate solvent.
  2. Allow the paper to dry, then apply a locating agent (for example, ninhydrin for amino acids).
  3. The agent makes initially invisible spots appear coloured, sometimes after warming.
  4. Visible dyes do not normally need a locating agent.

Why each option is right or wrong

  • A. Correct: colourless spots need a locating agent to be seen.
  • B. Insolubility does not itself indicate a locating agent is needed; the sample may not move with the solvent.
  • C. Different-coloured substances are already visible, whether or not they have matching Rf values.
  • D. Same colour does not make spots invisible; a locating agent is not required simply for that reason.

Exam key idea: Locating agents are used to reveal colourless chromatogram spots.

title: A blue solid, Q, is soluble in water.
context: Which method is used to obtain pure solid Q from aqueous solution?
explanation:
Crystallisation recovers a dissolved solid as purified crystals.

Step-by-step reasoning

  1. Gently evaporate some water until the solution is nearly saturated.
  2. Allow the concentrated solution to cool to grow crystals.
  3. Filter the crystals and dry them carefully.
  4. Filtration alone cannot separate a dissolved solute from its aqueous solution.

Why each option is right or wrong

  • A. Chromatography is principally used to separate dissolved components in mixtures.
  • B. Correct: crystallisation yields pure crystals of Q.
  • C. The dissolved solid would pass through filter paper.
  • D. Neutralisation is a reaction between an acid and base, not a separation method for this solution.

Exam key idea: Dissolved solid → concentrate solution → cool → crystals.

title: Two test-tubes each contain a sample of water. One test-tube contains pure water, but the other test-tube contains water and dissolved sodium chloride as an impurity.
context:
Which tests may be used to identify the test-tube that contains pure water?

  1. Measure the boiling point of each water sample.
  2. Test each sample with acidified aqueous silver nitrate.
  3. Test each sample with anhydrous copper(II) sulfate.
explanation:
Boiling point and the chloride ion test can distinguish pure water from salt water. Anhydrous copper(II) sulfate detects water in either sample.

Step-by-step reasoning

  1. Pure water boils sharply at 100 °C at standard atmospheric pressure; dissolved sodium chloride raises its boiling point.
  2. Acidified silver nitrate forms a white AgCl precipitate with chloride ions in the sodium chloride solution.
  3. Anhydrous CuSO₄ changes from white to blue with both samples, because both contain water.
  4. Therefore tests 1 and 2 can distinguish the samples, but test 3 cannot.

Why each option is right or wrong

  • A. Correct: boiling-point comparison and AgNO₃ distinguish pure and salty water.
  • B. Incomplete: the chloride test also works.
  • C. Incorrect: CuSO₄ detects water in both, so 3 does not distinguish purity.
  • D. Incorrect: test 3 is the same positive water test for both samples.

Exam key idea: Testing for the presence of water does not prove water is pure.

title: The results of some tests on dilute aqueous solution X are shown.
context:
testobservation
add aqueous ammonia dropwisewhite precipitate
then add aqueous ammonia in excessprecipitate dissolves to form colourless solution
add aqueous sodium hydroxide dropwisewhite precipitate
then add aqueous sodium hydroxide in excessprecipitate dissolves to form colourless solution

Which cation is present in X?
explanation:
Zn²⁺ forms a white precipitate that dissolves in excess aqueous ammonia and also in excess sodium hydroxide.

Step-by-step reasoning

  1. Adding either alkali dropwise produces a white precipitate of zinc hydroxide, Zn(OH)₂.
  2. Excess sodium hydroxide dissolves Zn(OH)₂ to form colourless zincate complexes.
  3. Excess aqueous ammonia also dissolves the precipitate, forming a colourless ammine complex.
  4. This behaviour is characteristic of Zn²⁺ among the four choices.

Why each option is right or wrong

  • A. Al³⁺ gives a white precipitate soluble in excess NaOH but insoluble in excess ammonia.
  • B. Ca²⁺ does not show a white precipitate soluble in excess of both reagents.
  • C. Cr³⁺ typically forms a grey-green precipitate, not the observed white one.
  • D. Correct: Zn²⁺ dissolves in excess ammonia and excess NaOH.

Exam key idea: Zn²⁺: white precipitate, soluble in excess NH₃ and in excess NaOH.

title: Which diagram shows the direction of movement of ions and electrons during the electrolysis of molten sodium chloride?
explanation:
In molten sodium chloride, Na⁺ ions move towards the negative cathode and Cl⁻ ions move towards the positive anode. Electrons travel through the external circuit, not through the molten electrolyte.

Step-by-step explanation

  1. NaCl(l) contains mobile Na⁺ and Cl⁻ ions.
  2. At the cathode, Na⁺ gains electrons: Na⁺ + e⁻ → Na.
  3. At the anode, chloride ions lose electrons: 2Cl⁻ → Cl₂ + 2e⁻.
  4. Diagram A correctly shows the electrode labels, ion motion and electron arrows.

Check each answer

  • A. Correct: Na⁺ moves left to the cathode, Cl⁻ moves right to the anode, and the electron directions are shown correctly.
  • B. The ions move towards the wrong electrodes.
  • C. The electrodes are swapped relative to the directions of ion movement.
  • D. Both the electrode labels and ion movement are inconsistent.

Exam key idea: Cations → cathode (reduction); anions → anode (oxidation).

title: Which statement about hydrogen fuel cells is correct?
options: Hydrogen fuel cells produce water as the only product.
Hydrogen fuel cells do not need oxygen.
The waste from a hydrogen fuel cell is an acidic gas.
The reaction in a fuel cell is endothermic.
answer: A. Hydrogen fuel cells produce water as the only product.
explanation:
In a hydrogen–oxygen fuel cell, the overall chemical product is water. Chemical energy is converted to electrical energy.

Step-by-step explanation

  1. Hydrogen enters the fuel cell as the fuel and oxygen is required as the oxidant.
  2. The overall reaction is 2H₂ + O₂ → 2H₂O.
  3. Electricity and heat are released; the chemical reaction is exothermic.

Check each answer

  • A. Correct: water is the only chemical reaction product in a hydrogen–oxygen cell.
  • B. Oxygen is required as the oxidising reactant.
  • C. Water is not an acidic gas.
  • D. The overall reaction releases energy; it is not endothermic.

Exam key idea: Hydrogen fuel cell: hydrogen + oxygen → water, producing electrical energy.

title: Which equation represents an endothermic reaction?
explanation:
Breaking a chemical bond requires energy. Splitting Cl₂ into two separate chlorine atoms absorbs energy and is endothermic.

Step-by-step explanation

  1. Cl₂ has a covalent Cl–Cl bond.
  2. Cl₂(g) → 2Cl(g) represents bond breaking, requiring energy input.
  3. Bond formation releases energy, as do combustion and reactive Group I metal–water reactions.

Check each answer

  • A. Combustion of methane is exothermic.
  • B. Correct: splitting Cl₂ molecules breaks a bond and absorbs energy.
  • C. Bond formation between hydrogen atoms releases energy.
  • D. The reaction of potassium with water releases heat.

Exam key idea: Bond breaking = endothermic; bond formation = exothermic.

chapter: Chemical Energetics · Catalysts and activation energy
title: The diagram shows the reaction pathway diagram for the reaction between X and Y to form product Z.
context:
The reaction happens more rapidly if a catalyst is used.

How would the diagram change when a catalyst is used?
options: The arrow representing E<sub>a</sub> would be larger.
The arrow representing E<sub>a</sub> would be smaller.
The arrow representing ΔH would be larger.
The arrow representing ΔH would be smaller.
answer: B. The arrow representing E<sub>a</sub> would be smaller.
explanation:
A catalyst provides an alternative reaction pathway with lower activation energy, Eₐ. It does not change the energy difference ΔH between the reactants and products.

Step-by-step explanation

  1. Activation energy is the energy barrier from reactants to the transition state.
  2. A catalyst makes this barrier lower, so a greater proportion of collisions are successful.
  3. The reactant and product energy levels stay unchanged, so ΔH does not change.

Check each answer

  • A. A catalyst reduces, rather than increases, activation energy.
  • B. Correct: the Eₐ arrow becomes smaller.
  • C. ΔH remains unchanged by a catalyst.
  • D. ΔH remains unchanged by a catalyst.

Exam key idea: Catalyst: lowers Eₐ; does not change ΔH.

title: In a reaction, element J acts as an oxidising agent.
context:
Which statements about J are correct?

  1. J is oxidised.
  2. J gains electrons.
  3. J loses electrons.
  4. The oxidation number of J decreases.
explanation:
An oxidising agent oxidises another substance and is itself reduced. Reduction involves gaining electrons and a decrease in oxidation number.

Step-by-step explanation

  1. When J accepts electrons, it causes another species to lose electrons.
  2. Therefore J undergoes reduction, not oxidation.
  3. Statements 2 and 4 are both correct.

Check each answer

  • A. Statement 1 is false: J is reduced.
  • B. Both statements 1 and 3 are false for an oxidising agent.
  • C. Correct: J gains electrons and its oxidation number decreases.
  • D. Statement 3 is false because J gains rather than loses electrons.

Exam key idea: Oxidising agent → gains electrons → oxidation number decreases.

chapter: Reversible Reactions · Haber and Contact processes
title: Four statements about the Haber process and the Contact process are listed.
context:
1. Both processes are carried out at 200 kPa.
  2. Both processes are carried out at 450 °C.
  3. Both processes use a reactant that is extracted from air.
  4. Both processes use iron as a catalyst.

Which two statements are correct?
explanation:
Both industrial processes operate at about 450 °C and use a component of air. The Haber process uses nitrogen, whereas the Contact process uses oxygen.

Step-by-step explanation

  1. Haber process: N₂ + 3H₂ ⇌ 2NH₃, with an iron catalyst, roughly 450 °C and high pressure (about 200 atmospheres).
  2. Contact process: 2SO₂ + O₂ ⇌ 2SO₃, with a vanadium(V) oxide catalyst, roughly 450 °C and low pressure.
  3. Statement 1 is false because 200 kPa (about 2 atm) is not the pressure used for the Haber process.
  4. Statement 4 is false because the Contact process uses V₂O₅ rather than iron.

Check each answer

  • A. Statement 1 is false.
  • B. Both statements 1 and 4 are false.
  • C. Correct: 2 and 3 are true.
  • D. Statement 4 is false.

Exam key idea: Common to both: ~450 °C and a reactant sourced from air.

title: Sodium hydroxide forms an alkaline solution.
context: Which indicator turns yellow when added to this solution?
explanation:
Methyl orange is yellow in alkaline solution. The other indicators listed have different colours in alkalis.

Step-by-step explanation

  1. NaOH(aq) is an alkali containing OH⁻ ions.
  2. Methyl orange changes to yellow in alkaline conditions.
  3. Litmus is blue, thymolphthalein is blue (at sufficiently high pH), and universal indicator is blue–purple in alkaline NaOH.

Check each answer

  • A. Litmus turns blue, not yellow.
  • B. Correct: methyl orange is yellow in alkaline solution.
  • C. Thymolphthalein turns blue in sufficiently alkaline solution.
  • D. Universal indicator is blue or purple in strongly alkaline solution.

Exam key idea: Methyl orange: red in acid, yellow in alkali.

chapter: Acids Bases and Salts · Strong acids
title: What is the definition of a strong acid?
options: It is a proton acceptor that is completely dissociated in aqueous solution.
It is a proton acceptor that is partially dissociated in aqueous solution.
It is a proton donor that is completely dissociated in aqueous solution.
It is a proton donor that is partially dissociated in aqueous solution.
answer: C. It is a proton donor that is completely dissociated in aqueous solution.
explanation:
A strong acid is a proton donor that completely ionises in aqueous solution. Strength refers to degree of ionisation, not concentration.

Step-by-step explanation

  1. Acids donate H⁺ ions (protons); bases accept protons.
  2. A strong acid dissociates almost completely into ions in water.
  3. A weak acid ionises only partially.

Check each answer

  • A. Proton acceptor describes a base.
  • B. Proton acceptor describes a base, and partial dissociation does not describe a strong acid.
  • C. Correct: proton donor with complete dissociation.
  • D. A proton donor that partially dissociates is a weak acid.

Exam key idea: Strong acids are fully dissociated in water; weak acids are only partially dissociated.

chapter: Acids Bases and Salts · Amphoteric oxides
title: Tin(II) oxide, SnO, is amphoteric.
context:
Which reactions show that tin(II) oxide is amphoteric?

  1. 4SnO → 2SnO2 + 2Sn
  2. SnO + 2HCl → SnCl2 + H2O
  3. 2SnO + O2 → 2SnO2
  4. SnO + 2NaOH → Na2SnO2 + H2O
explanation:
An amphoteric oxide reacts with both acids and alkalis. SnO reacts with hydrochloric acid in equation 2 and sodium hydroxide in equation 4.

Step-by-step explanation

  1. Equation 2 shows SnO reacting with an acid, HCl.
  2. Equation 4 shows SnO reacting with an alkali, NaOH.
  3. Equation 1 is disproportionation and equation 3 is oxidation, so neither alone demonstrates amphoteric behaviour.

Check each answer

  • A. Reaction 1 is not an acid–base reaction showing amphoterism.
  • B. Neither 1 nor 3 shows reaction with acid and alkali.
  • C. Equation 3 is oxidation, not reaction with an alkali.
  • D. Correct: SnO reacts with acid (2) and alkali (4).

Exam key idea: Amphoteric = reacts with both acids and bases/alkalis.

chapter: Acids Bases and Salts · Water of crystallisation
title: Which statement defines the term water of crystallisation?
options: the water molecules removed from a solution when a crystalline substance is formed
the water required to dissolve a crystalline substance to make a solution
the water molecules present in a hydrated crystalline solid
the water added to a hydrated crystallised solid to make it anhydrous
answer: C. the water molecules present in a hydrated crystalline solid
explanation:
Water of crystallisation consists of water molecules incorporated into the crystalline structure of a hydrated salt.

Step-by-step explanation

  1. Hydrated crystals have a fixed number of water molecules per formula unit.
  2. For example, CuSO₄·5H₂O contains five water molecules of crystallisation for each CuSO₄ formula unit.
  3. On heating, a hydrated salt may lose water of crystallisation and become anhydrous.

Check each answer

  • A. This describes water leaving the solution, not water inside the crystals.
  • B. This is solvent used for dissolving, not water of crystallisation.
  • C. Correct: water present as part of the hydrated crystal.
  • D. Adding water does not make a substance anhydrous; removing water does.

Exam key idea: Hydrated salt = anhydrous salt + water of crystallisation.

title: When water evaporates from a brass surface, the temperature of the brass surface decreases.
context: Which row describes this evaporation process?
options: endothermic; from the brass surface to the water
endothermic; from the water to the brass surface
exothermic; from the brass surface to the water
exothermic; from the water to the brass surface
answer: A. endothermic; from the brass surface to the water
explanation:
Evaporation is endothermic. The evaporating water absorbs thermal energy from the brass, cooling the brass surface.

Step-by-step explanation

  1. Water molecules need energy to escape from the liquid into the gas state.
  2. The energy flows from the brass surface to the water.
  3. The brass loses thermal energy, so its temperature decreases.
  4. Therefore the correct combination is endothermic, from brass to water.

Check each option

  • A. Correct: evaporation requires energy supplied by the brass surface.
  • B. The process is endothermic, but this reverses the actual direction of thermal-energy transfer.
  • C. The direction is correct, but evaporation is not exothermic.
  • D. Both the process type and energy-transfer direction are incorrect.

Exam key idea: Evaporation absorbs energy from the surrounding surface.
tableHeaders: direction of transfer of thermal energy
tableRows: from the brass surface to the water
from the water to the brass surface
from the brass surface to the water
from the water to the brass surface

title: A solid lump of tin is heated until it melts.
context:
Which statements describe what happens when solid tin melts?

  1. The atoms of tin move further apart.
  2. The atoms of tin lose thermal energy to the surroundings.
  3. The atoms of tin gain thermal energy from the surroundings.
  4. The temperature of the tin increases.
explanation:
Melting is an endothermic change of state. Tin takes in thermal energy while its atoms become less ordered and typically slightly further apart.

Step-by-step explanation

  1. During melting, energy is absorbed from the surroundings, making statement 3 correct.
  2. Atoms become able to move relative to each other, and tin expands on melting, making statement 1 correct.
  3. During the change of state itself, the temperature stays constant at its melting point, so statement 4 is false.
  4. Statement 2 is false because tin gains, rather than loses, thermal energy.

Check each option

  • A. Statement 1 is correct, but statement 2 is not.
  • B. Correct: statements 1 and 3.
  • C. Statements 2 and 4 are false for melting.
  • D. Statement 3 is correct, but statement 4 is false during the phase change.

Exam key idea: For a pure substance, temperature remains constant while it melts; energy is absorbed to change state.

title: A gas is placed in a sealed container.
context:
The gas has a pressure of one atmosphere and a temperature of 50 °C.

It is then heated to 100 °C.

Which row describes the cause of the pressure of the gas and the effect of increasing the temperature of the gas?
options: collisions between gas particles and other gas particles; collisions become less frequent
collisions between gas particles and other gas particles; the average velocity of the gas particles increases
collisions between gas particles and the sides of the container; collisions between gas particles and other gas particles become less frequent
collisions between gas particles and the sides of the container; the average velocity of the gas particles increases
answer: D. collisions between gas particles and the sides of the container; the average velocity of the gas particles increases
explanation:
Gas pressure comes from gas particles colliding with the walls of the container. Higher temperature increases their average speed.

Step-by-step explanation

  1. Gas particles collide randomly with the inside walls, transferring momentum and producing pressure.
  2. Heating raises the average kinetic energy and hence the mean particle speed.
  3. In a rigid container, particles strike the walls harder and more frequently, increasing pressure.
  4. The correct cause and effect are both described by row D.

Check each option

  • A. Gas–gas collisions are not the direct cause of the pressure exerted on the container walls.
  • B. It correctly predicts increased speed, but misidentifies the cause of pressure.
  • C. Pressure is due to wall collisions, but heating does not make gas-particle collisions less frequent in a rigid container.
  • D. Correct: wall collisions cause pressure, and average speed rises on heating.

Exam key idea: Gas pressure = collisions with walls; heating raises average particle kinetic energy.

title: A sample of element X has two isotopes.
context:
The symbols for the two isotopes are 63X and 65X.

The relative abundance of 65X is 25.0%.

What is the relative atomic mass of X?
explanation:
Relative atomic mass is the weighted average of the isotope masses. The 65 isotope accounts for 25%, so the 63 isotope accounts for 75%.

Step-by-step explanation

  1. Abundance of ⁶³X = 100 − 25 = 75%.
  2. Weighted average = (63 × 75 + 65 × 25) ÷ 100.
  3. = (4725 + 1625) ÷ 100 = 63.5.

Check each option

  • A. Correct: 63.5 is the abundance-weighted average.
  • B. 63.7 comes from an incorrect weighting or arithmetic.
  • C. 64.0 is the midpoint but the two isotopes do not occur in equal proportions.
  • D. 64.5 overweights the heavier isotope.

Exam key idea: Always weight each isotope mass by its percentage abundance.

title: Which statement about magnesium chloride, MgCl₂, is correct?
options: Molten magnesium chloride conducts electricity because its electrons are free to move.
It consists of anions and cations which have completely filled outer electron shells.
It has a high melting point because its covalent bonds are very strong.
The magnesium ions and chloride ions are bonded together by delocalised electrons.
answer: B. It consists of anions and cations which have completely filled outer electron shells.
explanation:
Magnesium chloride has a giant ionic structure of Mg²⁺ and Cl⁻ ions. The ions have full outer electron shells.

Step-by-step explanation

  1. A magnesium atom loses two electrons to become Mg²⁺.
  2. Two chlorine atoms each gain one electron, giving two Cl⁻ ions.
  3. The ions have stable outer-shell electron configurations.
  4. Molten MgCl₂ conducts because ions move; its high melting point results from strong electrostatic attraction between ions.

Check each option

  • A. Molten ionic substances conduct using mobile ions, not free electrons.
  • B. Correct: the cations and anions have filled outer electron shells.
  • C. MgCl₂ is ionic, not a giant covalent structure.
  • D. Delocalised electrons describe metallic bonding, not ionic bonding.

Exam key idea: Ionic bonds = electrostatic attraction between oppositely charged ions; mobile ions conduct when molten.

title: Which row describes the structure of a solid metal and explains the property?
options: lattice of negative ions in a sea of electrons; conducts electricity because the electrons are free to move
lattice of negative ions in a sea of electrons; is malleable because the layers of ions can slide over each other
lattice of positive ions in a sea of electrons; conducts electricity because the ions are free to move
lattice of positive ions in a sea of electrons; is malleable because the layers of ions can slide over each other
answer: D. lattice of positive ions in a sea of electrons; is malleable because the layers of ions can slide over each other
explanation:
A metal contains a regular lattice of positive ions surrounded by delocalised electrons. Its layers of ions can slide, so metals are malleable.

Step-by-step explanation

  1. Metal atoms form a lattice of positive ions with delocalised electrons between them.
  2. Mobile electrons carry electricity, while the positive ions remain in lattice positions in the solid.
  3. Layers of positive ions can slide while metallic attraction is maintained.
  4. Row D combines the correct structure with a correct explanation of malleability.

Check each option

  • A. Positive, not negative, metal ions form the lattice.
  • B. The lattice ions are positive rather than negative.
  • C. The stated lattice is correct, but electrical conduction comes from mobile delocalised electrons, not mobile ions.
  • D. Correct: positive-ion lattice; movable layers explain malleability.

Exam key idea: Solid metals conduct through mobile electrons and are malleable because ion layers can slide.

title: Which atom or ion has the electronic configuration 2,8,8?
explanation:
2,8,8 represents 18 electrons. Calcium has 20 electrons as a neutral atom, but Ca²⁺ has lost two and therefore has 18.

Step-by-step explanation

  1. Add the electrons: 2 + 8 + 8 = 18.
  2. Ne has 10 electrons; Na⁺ has 10; Br⁻ has 36.
  3. Calcium has proton number 20 and Ca²⁺ has 20 − 2 = 18 electrons.

Check each option

  • A. Ne has 10 electrons (2,8).
  • B. Na⁺ has 10 electrons (2,8).
  • C. Br⁻ has 36 electrons (2,8,18,8).
  • D. Correct: Ca²⁺ has 18 electrons (2,8,8).

Exam key idea: For a cation subtract lost electrons; for an anion add gained electrons.

title: The formula of a compound containing element Z is Na₂Z₂O₃.
context:
The relative formula mass of the compound is 158.

What is the relative atomic mass of Z?
explanation:
Use the relative formula mass and subtract the known sodium and oxygen contributions.

Step-by-step explanation

  1. Mᵣ = 2Aᵣ(Na) + 2Aᵣ(Z) + 3Aᵣ(O).
  2. 158 = 2(23) + 2Z + 3(16) = 46 + 2Z + 48.
  3. 158 = 94 + 2Z, so 2Z = 64 and Z = 32.

Check each option

  • A. Correct: 32.
  • B. 59.5 comes from incorrectly accounting for the atom counts.
  • C. 64 is the mass of two Z atoms, not one Z atom.
  • D. 119 results from incorrect substitution or atom counting.

Exam key idea: Multiply Aᵣ by subscripts, then divide the remaining mass by the number of unknown atoms.

title: Magnesium reacts with steam to form hydrogen.
context:
Mg + H2O → MgO + H2

How many molecules of hydrogen gas are made when 3.6 g of magnesium are heated with 1.8 g of steam?

(Assume Avogadro's constant = 6 × 1023 and the yield of magnesium oxide is 100%.)
explanation:
Steam is the limiting reactant. The balanced equation uses 1 mol of steam to make 1 mol of hydrogen.

Step-by-step explanation

  1. Moles Mg = 3.6 ÷ 24 = 0.15 mol.
  2. Moles H₂O = 1.8 ÷ 18 = 0.10 mol.
  3. The reaction ratio is 1:1, so 0.10 mol H₂ is produced.
  4. Hydrogen molecules = 0.10 × 6 × 10²³ = 6 × 10²².

Check each option

  • A. Correct: 6 × 10²² molecules from 0.10 mol H₂.
  • B. This counts twice as many hydrogen molecules as the limiting reactant permits.
  • C. 9 × 10²² is based on the magnesium amount (0.15 mol) without applying the limiting reactant.
  • D. 18 × 10²² overestimates product formation.

Exam key idea: Calculate both reactant mole amounts; the smaller stoichiometric supply limits the product.

title: Compound Y contains 48.65% carbon, 8.10% hydrogen and 43.25% oxygen by mass.
context: What is the empirical formula of compound Y?
explanation:
Convert percentages into moles and simplify to the smallest whole-number ratio.

Step-by-step explanation

  1. Treat the percentages as masses in 100 g.
  2. C: 48.65 ÷ 12 = 4.054; H: 8.10 ÷ 1 = 8.10; O: 43.25 ÷ 16 = 2.703.
  3. Divide by 2.703: C ≈ 1.5, H ≈ 3, O = 1.
  4. Multiply all by 2: C : H : O = 3 : 6 : 2. Thus C₃H₆O₂.

Check each option

  • A. This gives a hydrogen ratio too small.
  • B. This is not the simplified whole-number ratio of the three elements.
  • C. This has an incorrect carbon-to-oxygen ratio.
  • D. Correct: C₃H₆O₂ is the lowest whole-number mole ratio.

Exam key idea: Percent ÷ Aᵣ → mole ratio → divide by smallest → whole numbers.

title: Calcium carbonate is reacted with an excess of dilute hydrochloric acid.
context:
CaCO3 + 2HCl → CaCl2 + H2O + CO2

Which two changes, when applied together, will increase both the rate of reaction and the volume of carbon dioxide produced?
options: increasing the concentration of hydrochloric acid and adding a catalyst
increasing the volume of hydrochloric acid and the temperature of the reaction
increasing the mass of calcium carbonate and the temperature of the reaction
increasing the surface area of the calcium carbonate and adding a catalyst
answer: C. increasing the mass of calcium carbonate and the temperature of the reaction
explanation:
More calcium carbonate produces more CO₂, while higher temperature makes the reaction faster. The hydrochloric acid is already in excess.

Step-by-step explanation

  1. The quantity of limiting calcium carbonate determines the total moles of CO₂.
  2. Adding more CaCO₃ increases the total amount of gas that can form, as long as HCl remains in excess.
  3. Increasing temperature makes a greater fraction of collisions energetic enough to react, so the rate increases.
  4. A catalyst or greater surface area only changes the rate, not total gas formed from a fixed amount of CaCO₃.

Check each option

  • A. Both changes may speed reaction, but neither increases gas yield with fixed CaCO₃.
  • B. With hydrochloric acid already in excess, adding extra acid does not increase total CO₂.
  • C. Correct: more CaCO₃ raises gas volume and higher temperature raises rate.
  • D. These changes raise rate but not the total CO₂ from an unchanged amount of CaCO₃.

Exam key idea: Rate and total yield are different; identify the limiting reactant.

title: Concentrated aqueous sodium chloride and dilute sulfuric acid are electrolysed with inert electrodes.
context: Which row describes the electrode products for each electrolyte?
explanation:
Concentrated sodium chloride solution produces hydrogen at the cathode and chlorine at the anode. Dilute sulfuric acid produces hydrogen at the cathode and oxygen at the anode.

Step-by-step explanation

  1. At the cathode (negative), reduction produces hydrogen from aqueous ions.
  2. In concentrated NaCl(aq), chloride ions are oxidised to chlorine gas at the anode (positive).
  3. In dilute H₂SO₄(aq), water is oxidised to oxygen at the anode.
  4. Therefore the products are H₂ / Cl₂ for brine and H₂ / O₂ for sulfuric acid.

Check each option

  • A. The electrodes for brine are swapped.
  • B. Correct: brine H₂/Cl₂; dilute acid H₂/O₂.
  • C. The electrode products are swapped in both cases.
  • D. The dilute sulfuric acid cathode and anode products are reversed.

Exam key idea: Electrolysis with inert electrodes: brine → H₂ + Cl₂; dilute sulfuric acid → H₂ + O₂.
